angle: When a museum strips the wall text and calls the result 'open to interpretation,' does removing the label actually remove the informational hierarchy — or does it just make the default channel invisible, so that whoever the room already served keeps reading it and whoever needed the words is now demoted to guessing?

correction_moment.editorial_need: Pixel arrives expecting 'no label' to be the purest failure of visual information hierarchy — the piece is stronger if the material forces her to see that shrinking or relocating text can be just as much a hierarchy decision as deleting it, complicating her 'blank wall = worst case' instinct.

evidence_candidate.source_excerpt: Labels mounted at eye level were found to be read far more often than those placed above or below it.

correction_moment.interpretation: If placement alone — eye level versus above or below — swings whether a label is read at all, then the fight was never label-versus-no-label; it was already hierarchy all the way down, and a present label mounted wrong is functionally a blank wall too. That breaks Pixel's clean binary and forces her to argue about degrees of demotion rather than presence versus absence.

cross_cite: The claim that the primary failure here is one of information architecture — what channel carries the meaning and who can access it — presses against the view that the room's real politics live in its acoustic and spatial texture; the question is whether stripping the words even registers as loss to a visitor who was never navigating by them in the first place.
opening_scene: A blank wall is not the absence of an instruction; it is an instruction that only some visitors can read.

resisting_example.editorial_need: Pixel's suspicion of the app-and-fragment trend is that it displaces information into channels not everyone can reach; a resisting case from inside her own value system — someone framing minimal text as an opening rather than a withholding — keeps her from writing the easy grievance.

evidence_candidate.direct_quote: the beginning of a relationship, not the end of an explanation
evidence_candidate.source_excerpt: a museum representative described the printed label itself as 'the beginning of a relationship, not the end of an explanation.'

resisting_example.interpretation: This is the hardest version of the opposing view for Pixel to defeat, because it isn't defending less information — it's claiming the wall was never meant to carry the whole load, that hierarchy is supposed to route depth elsewhere. She has to decide whether that routing is generous design or just exclusion relocated to a channel with an entry fee (a phone, an app, a hand free to hold it).

seed_sentence: A blank wall is not the absence of an instruction; it is an instruction that only some visitors can read.
